stories.headline: Herbert to undergo testing after exiting Chargers' 44-22 loss with finger injury
stories.summary: Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert, who was sacked eight times and threw his NFL-leading 11th interception, left Sunday's 44-22 loss to the Houston Texans in the second half with an injury to the middle finger on his left (non-throwing) hand.
stories.body:
Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert left Sunday's 44-22 loss to the Houston Texans in the fourth quarter with an injury to the middle finger on his left (non-throwing) hand.

Herbert said he wanted to stay in the game but coach Jim Harbaugh said he overruled the quarterback. The quarterback will undergo testing on the hand and Harbaugh said it "could be a fracture, we'll find out."

Herbert told reporters that he didn't believe the injury would be an issue for next week, when the Chargers play the Baltimore Ravens on "Monday Night Football."

He was sacked eight times in the loss and threw his NFL-leading 11th interception.

He did throw a touchdown pass, however, as the Chargers reached the end zone for the first time in three games.

The Chargers fell to 0-8 on the season with the loss.

stories.headline: Wet weather mastery of Norris, Verstappen make Brazil F1's must-see race
stories.summary: Max Verstappen is known for excelling in the rain, but in winning Sunday's wet Brazilian Grand Prix, Lando Norris proved he deserves accolades too.
stories.body:
SÃO PAULO -- After a week of plaudits for Kimi Antonelli, it was his predecessors Lando Norris and Max Verstappen who turned in two very different kinds of champions' drives in the rain at Interlagos, which again proved why it has become such a popular and integral part of Formula 1's calendar.

On the grid ahead of Sunday's Brazilian Grand Prix, it felt like all the ingredients of a guaranteed box-office classic were there: the twists and turns of the Interlagos circuit, changing weather in the São Paulo sky, and the prospect of Verstappen at the back of the field with a brand-new engine, perfectly placed to add to his long list of epic wet-weather drives. As is so often the case with Brazil's popular grand prix -- which will be staying on the calendar until 2035 after securing an extension this weekend -- it delivered.

The story of the opening lap centered around the grid's four world champions.

On a wet but slowly drying track, Norris' slow getaway allowed Antonelli to charge down into Turn 1 in the lead, with Norris then losing position to a superb Liam Lawson move around the outside. At the back end of the grid was box-office stuff. The timing screen initially seemed to be showing Lewis Hamilton and Verstappen rising through the order as though in error -- the pair were scything through the pack like knives through butter. By the end of the lap one, Hamilton (who, like Verstappen, came into the race with a big engine penalty) had gained 11 places to ninth, while Verstappen had gained 10 places to 12th.

Both of those things at either end of the grid set the tone for what would come later, with Antonelli and Norris finding their afternoons going in opposite directions as the race unfolded from there, and Hamilton and Verstappen's monster starts unfolding very differently in the laps that followed.

Norris' dominant drive
Norris would later joke he could not repeat what he thought when Lawson got past him, as he would likely get fined. That's perhaps not surprising given how much of an opportunity the race had appeared to be. A masterful pole position on Saturday and the changing weather seemed like a perfect way for Norris to fight for his and McLaren's third win of the year.

The key moment came on lap 20.

Norris, who had crucially pitted one lap earlier to make the crucial swap from intermediate wet to the soft dry tire, was reaping the benefits of tires that had gotten up to temperature much quicker. Antonelli, by contrast, was struggling massively, suddenly finding a curiously imbalanced car that he lost all confidence in. Suddenly rattled and spooked by his misbehaving car, Antonelli looked wobbly out on track, meaning what followed felt somewhat inevitable. As they approached Turn 1, the Italian spun and lost the lead, letting Norris by.

"I forced Kimi to push, he went into a mistake I could capitalize on," Norris said later.

From there, he was impervious, turning in a faultless drive to claim his third win of the season, nearly 15 seconds up the road on Verstappen by the checkered flag. The Red Bull driver had started from the back of the field but appeared to have at least muscled his way back into the contest by mid-distance as he passed teammate Isack Hadjar into second. Even once that had happened, Norris was untouchable out in front -- whether it was on the intermediates when the track was wet, or on the slicks when the track was dry, Norris had Verstappen's number when it came to pace.

"It's up there [with my best wins] in terms of challenge to achieve," Norris said after the contest. "Not been easy for all reasons possible! Conditions, weather, important to not make mistakes. A lot thrown at everyone on a day like today, but probably our best race in terms of execution ... From my side not making any mistakes, which is so easy to do. Great performance from the team."

It was a fitting venue to do it, too. Norris still has the No. 1 on his car but lost his status as defending world champion seven days earlier. Interlagos also provided an easy example for critics to knock him in the past -- his nightmarish, error-strewn race in 2024 felt at the time like it might end up being career-defining, and the fact it contrasted so strongly with Verstappen's famous charge from the back of the field to victory in the pouring rain, a result that effectively ended Norris' hopes of beating the Dutchman to the title, seemed to just underline their difference in that type of weather.

The following two visits to Interlagos have undone that reputational damage. Norris' 2025 double of the sprint and grand prix victories were a hammer blow to struggling teammate Oscar Piastri last season, and this year came in treacherous conditions on a knife edge.

McLaren boss Andrea Stella said it highlighted where Norris had blossomed into a far more rounded driver.

"When Lando operates at his best, he's definitely one of the best drivers on the grid," Stella said on Sunday evening. "And we have seen that in these conditions, like yesterday, it's not the first time that when you have mixed variable conditions, he kind of is one of the fastest in finding the limit. And you have seen this today as well when the track was in the middle between dry and wet, it was when he was probably gaining most throughout the races on anybody else. I think he's very sensitive in understanding how much grip is available and very complete as a driver from a technical point of view, in terms of understanding how to deploy his tools to use the grip that is available."

Stella suggested these are traits of Norris that do not get the recognition that often goes to his rivals.

"Adaptability is actually probably the most important feature that you may want to possess as a driver," the McLaren team principal said. "I think that's one that should be definitely acknowledged and recognized for Lando. When there's a need to understand what's best, how to operate, he's definitely a master.

"And hopefully, let me say, we don't need to [always] rely on these qualities. We just want to make sure that we can offer Lando and Oscar a competitive car, such that they can just drive a little bit more easily, because still our car remains pretty difficult."

Norris will look to end his title-defense season on a high from here, with three races to go. It has been a frustrating year, which started with an uncompetitive and unreliable McLaren, and featured a brief flurry as a title outsider when he won races either side of the summer break in Hungary and the Netherlands.

Max the rain master
While Norris might not always get the plaudits for what he can do in changeable conditions, there has never been much doubt over what Verstappen is capable of when presented with stormy skies and a wet track. It's why most who ESPN asked on Sunday in the paddock still fancied Verstappen as a contender for victory before the race, despite the fact his view at the start was of 20 other cars parked in front of him on the sloped start-finish straight. Lining up directly ahead of him, just to make things feel really exciting, was his old 2021 foe Hamilton, a man just as renowned for wet-weather brilliance.

While both charged up the order in a stunning first lap, it initially looked like Hamilton was about to deliver something legendary in his red Ferrari. Despite the progress he was making a little way back, Verstappen had found himself frustrated.

"To be honest, I had a very slow reaction time off the line because I was holding the clutch wrong, so I had to react very quickly," Verstappen admitted later. "Then I was slow off the line, and that was my mistake. But then I just got a bit unlucky in the first three corners, where it was just like a traffic jam. There were three or four cars in front blocking basically how much I could pass. Actually, Lewis had a very good first lap. He could really get through those cars, so I was a little bit disappointed that I couldn't make the same headway. But then, within two laps, I was just flying by cars, almost every corner. We had a lot more grip, I guess, than most in the midfield. I don't know what lap I was in the top 10, but it all happened very quickly."

As Verstappen's tires came to life, Hamilton's did the opposite, and he soon dropped down the order.

"I had a great start, and I thought I was on for something positive, then the tires dropped off almost immediately as the track dried," Hamilton explained later. "It's really hard to then stay on the track. Just massive challenges with getting the tires in the window and having them working ... We didn't get the points I think the team deserved today. I definitely take some of that on me today."

Verstappen kicked on, getting past Hamilton for ninth at the final corner as the Ferrari wobbled left and right. The Red Bull driver's passes looked like a highlight reel of previous events -- Verstappen had won from the back of the pack in 2024 and finished third from the pit lane in 2025 and the early laps of his 2026 edition felt equally magical. His double overtake on Piastri and Williams' Alex Albon, especially, at Descida do Lago was the pick of a very competitive bunch.

As Antonelli also found in the Mercedes, the swap over to the dry tire killed the charge dead a little bit.

"As I switched to the slicks, I had an extreme amount of oversteer in the car in the high-speed corners, which made it super difficult to drive," Verstappen said. "So, we need to understand if something broke on the car, some kind of aero loss or whatever, because this was not normal."

Verstappen's second-place finish still deserved high praise, especially considering how his car had been performing. Onboard views made it clear he was fighting just to keep the car on the racetrack at points, with his faulty Red Bull radio only adding to the drama inside the cockpit. His post-race radio feedback to the pit wall summed up his mood.

"Yeah ... my god," he said. "Doing 85% of the race with a f---ed car. Of course P2 is nice, but not in this way. I'm sorry but what a disaster to drive. Unbelievable. I've never had something like this in the wet or the dry. Really, really bad."

It is perhaps a bad omen to the rest of the field for 2027 that, even with a car that is a "disaster" to drive, Verstappen still passed all but one other driver and finished second on the racetrack. If Red Bull start next year strongly and iron out the edges of its misbehaving car, Verstappen surely will be contending for a fifth world title before you know it.

Mercedes' odd weekend
Mercedes' race finished with Antonelli, George Russell and Toto Wolff surrounded by the entire race team on the podium, celebrating the constructors' title to Queen's "We Are The Champions." As with Antonelli's triumph at last weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix, that has been a matter of when, not if, for a while.

But the nature of the race that preceded those celebrations was odd.

Antonelli had come out of his first pit stop looking comfortable, but he quickly found himself in a car that seemed to be dancing left and right without much explanation. After the spin that cost him the lead, he would run wide again at Turn 1 and cede second place to Verstappen. Hadjar would quickly get by him as well.

It was perhaps a moment for the newly crowned champion to come crashing down to earth after his incredible past few weeks.

"I'm very disappointed for the race. I'm very angry to be fair, but I'm going to put all this aside for now because the team clinched the title," Antonelli said. "We clinched the title for the team, and they all deserve it and I'm very proud to be part of this group and this team who has done and still does so much for me and I'm very happy for them. But talking about the race specifically, yeah, very disappointing. We were on for the win up to that point. Also in the lead, once I was able to get some temperature I was getting to the rhythm. But yeah, the spin came which still is something I need to look at because I don't know why I lost the rear so quickly as well.

"Like no warning, nothing. But already to be fair when I put the soft, I felt something weird with the car. So, we need to check what happened but on the other hand yeah, shame because we lost the race there."

Mercedes might be doubly puzzled by the fact that Russell experienced exactly the same in the final stint. If Antonelli's race had been difficult, Russell's entire weekend had been even more so. The Englishman had finished Saturday's qualifying session raging at race engineer Marcus Dudley for telling him to back off a key Q3 push lap as the rain intensified, costing him first in qualifying. Russell's engine grid penalty knocked him down the order and he then lost any chance of competing for the win with an incredibly strange spin in the pit lane.

Russell, a man starved of positive moments of late, shouldered the blame later.

"Yeah, not really too sure what happened," he said. "I went quite high risk because I smelt an opportunity and paid the price. It's in those moments where you either gain a lot, or you lose a lot. This time it went against us."

There was a small moment of levity that followed that evening.

As Wolff spoke to the written press about Mercedes' title -- its first since 2021 -- Russell walked by as his boss was talking about planned celebrations. Wolff revealed Russell would be joining him on a private jet later where they would have a drink to the "good ... and some bad," a cheeky nod to Russell's ranting the day before. Russell, half way out of the door at that point, leant back inside, laughing, adding that he would be having more than one drink, repeating the "good and the bad" part.

Interlagos the perfect circuit of variables
A final word for one of the perfect Formula 1 race venues.

There's very little to find wrong with Interlagos. Its deal is to 2035, but it's difficult to imagine F1 ever being able to evade the fan anger that would surely follow any announcement that it was dropping off the calendar.

While it is a shame it no longer hosts races at the end of the calendar -- allowing it to host title-deciding contests in 2005, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009 and 2012 -- it has lost none of its penchant for drama and thrilling racing. It's a circuit featuring several good spots to overtake, treacherous weather, and anyone lucky enough to go will hear nothing but a carnival atmosphere throughout, with the fans seated all the way along the final corner right through to Turn 1 almost sitting on top of the banked, sloping racetrack.

The title climax of one week earlier might have taken some of the sting out of Sunday's contest, but Interlagos repeatedly delivers the goods. In a year that has featured a lot of very justified criticism over the state of F1's new cars and engines and the racing that has come with them, and in a year that featured the introduction of a new race at a place as dull and soulless as the Madring, F1 fans should be grateful Interlagos is here to stay for the foreseeable future.

stories.headline: AFL Draft: Key dates, FAQs, players to know, and more
stories.summary: The 2026 AFL draft is rapidly approaching, so here's your guide for what to know, including key dates and times, players to know, academy-linked names, and every club's pick.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL Draft is fast approaching. Marvel Stadium will once more play host to the first round at 7:00pm AEDT on November 19, with the draft recommencing for the second round onwards on November 20.

Key dates and times
Where: Marvel Stadium

How to watch: Fox Footy

First round: Thursday, November 19, 7pm AEDT

Second round onwards: Friday, November 20, 7pm AEDT

Preseason and rookie draft: Monday, November 23, 3pm AEDT

Each club's picks

*As at Nov. 9
Adelaide: 15, 32, 35, 43, 56, 92, 110

Brisbane: 21, 27, 28, 45, 79, 97, 115

Carlton: 13, 18, 31, 50, 61, 72, 90, 108

Collingwood: 1, 30, 67, 68, 70, 88, 106

Essendon: 1, 17, 25, 80, 98 (plus second round compensation pick)

Fremantle: 19, 40, 60, 63, 78, 96, 114

Geelong: 36, 57, 62, 75, 93, 111

Gold Coast: 8, 81, 85, 103

GWS: 9, 20, 26, 59, 77, 86, 104

Hawthorn: 29, 37, 71, 94, 107, 112

Melbourne: 4, 14, 48, 52

North Melbourne: 33, 49, 66, 74, 84, 102

Port Adelaide: 7, 12, 22, 24, 34, 46, 65, 101

Richmond: 2, 5, 44, 99 (plus second round compensation pick)

St Kilda: 10, 16, 41, 51, 69, 87, 105

Sydney: 6, 38, 39, 47, 54, 76, 95, 113

West Coast: 3, 23, 58, 64, 73, 82, 100 (plus second round compensation pick)

Western Bulldogs: 42, 53, 55, 83, 89, 91, 109

State of play and players to know
Essendon will be on the clock first, holding the top selection a decade on from the last time it took the number one pick to the AFL Draft. The Dons are expected to first bid on Port Adelaide-tied forward Dougie Cochrane, which will trigger a start-of-second-round compensation pick for the Bombers, Tigers and Eagles.

There are familial lines drawn throughout an exciting 2008-born cohort. Cody Walker is the son of high-flying Blue Andrew and will be headed to Princes Park. Cochrane is the son of former North Melbourne and Port Adelaide midfielder Stuart, though he isn't eligible to either team under the 100-game father-son rule. Instead, he's eligible to join the Power as part of their Next Generation Academy as an Indigenous prospect.

Top-10 riser Sam Gayfer is the nephew of 1990 premiership Pie Mick, and Koby LeCras brings goalkicking pedigree via 2018 premiership uncle Mark.

There will be up to five club-tied talents picked in the first round of the AFL Draft. But that won't necessarily result in an extended first night. Over the past five years the first round has averaged out to 25 selections accounting for father-son and academy bids, but clubs are expecting a number closer to the traditional 18 picks in the final intake of the 18-team competition.

Stricter stipulations around matching bids is at play, with clubs only able to use a maximum of two selections when matching for a club-tied prospect, meaning the selections of Port Adelaide, Carlton, Brisbane and GWS will be absorbed as early bids are matched.

We could see a record number of Indigenous talents picked in the first round. The high-water mark was four in 2005 and 2014, and all of Cochrane, Walker, Caylen Murray (Lions Academy), Toby Krasna and Jake Eime could be taken in the first round in 2026.

Thirteen of the top prospects have already been invited to Marvel Stadium on November 19.

Ethan Drever, Arki Butler and Heath Mellody are all still in contention to be the open pool No. 1 pick, with Harry Van Hattum, Gus Teixeira, Mitch Harris and Ethan Matthews (Giants Academy) rounding out the group on top of draft boards alongside Cochrane and Walker.

Murray, Gayfer, Wil Malady and Leo Steed have also received invites in a sign of club interest on night one.

Around 65 picks are expected to be taken across both nights which would surpass the 60 selections last year.

stories.headline: What if Manchester United had hired Jurgen Klopp?
stories.summary: If Manchester United hired an all-time great like Jurgen Klopp, would they have won the Premier League? Let's find out!
stories.body:
Right around this time every year, you can start to feel it. The air gets a little crisper. The shadows get a little colder. The days get shorter. The tree colors start to pop. You start wearing sweaters. Pumpkins appear in places where they do and do not belong.

Everyone and everything starts to shift, just slightly, in preparation for what's about to happen. The cycles of nature can be fickle and unpredictable, so the date is never exactly the same, and some years come and go without anything at all. But most years, it does.

Our tiny little rituals prime us to anticipate the inevitable, oncoming shift: that moment when Manchester United fire their manager and convince themselves that the new guy is finally going to be the one who fixes everything.

Ruben Amorim lost his job last January. Erik ten Hag was fired two years ago, right before Halloween. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer got the boot just a couple of days before Thanksgiving. And Jose Mourinho was relieved of his duties a little over a week before Christmas.

Now that we've once again entered the season of sacking, Michael Carrick seems like he will inevitably become the latest victim.

Man United are in the relegation zone. If history is any indication, their comeback against AS Roma in the Champions League will end up being meaningless. Before Tuesday's win, Carrick appeared to be on the verge of tears at the end of every match.

This is the 14th season since Manchester United last won the Premier League. And whoever replaces Carrick will be the ninth coach to try to do something that no other United manager since has done: just, simply, meet the expectations at one of the richest sports teams on the planet for more than a single season in a row.

But given how many different coaches have now failed since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club, it makes you wonder: Could anyone have been successful at Manchester United?

What is a great manager worth?

Arsenal won the Premier League last season with 85 points.

If we lived in a world where there were no subs and everyone on the field contributed exactly evenly to their team's success, then all 11 Arsenal players would have contributed about 8 points (7.7, to be slightly more exact) of value last season.

Except, the alternative to each player isn't just zero points. If you removed Bukayo Saka from the lineup, you wouldn't have to play a man down. No, you'd get to put another player out there who would also contribute to winning to some degree.

So, let's look at the relegation-level cutoff. West Ham were relegated with 39 points. Using the same framework, we'd say that all of their players were worth a little over 3.5 points across the season. We could then say that the average Arsenal player provided 5 more points of value than a relegation-level player.

This, of course, isn't exactly how it works: Some players are better than others, some positions are more valuable than others, and almost nobody plays 100% of the minutes. Goalkeeper David Raya played 97.3% of the league minutes last season, and Declan Rice led all outfield Gunners with 90.5% of minutes played.

But it all still gives us a nice benchmark. The best players on the best teams in the world are probably worth around 7 points more than your average relegation-level player. The truly generational superstars? You could probably bump that number up to 10 points if you wanted to.

But what about the manager? Rather than litigating the whole "managers don't matter" conversation for the 1,000th time on this website, we're just going to go with the logic put forth by Liverpool's former director of research, Ian Graham, in his book, "How to Win the Premier League": "[About] the same value as a good player brings. This is in line with manager salaries -- the best managers are paid a similar wage to the best players."

Who, then, was the best manager that Manchester United could've hired at any point over the past 14 seasons?

Most soccer-watchers would agree that there are two potential answers: Pep Guardiola or Jurgen Klopp. And most analyses would agree.

A 2025 study from the Sloan Sports Analytics conference looked at team performances from 2017 through 2024 across Europe's Big Five top leagues. The study awarded or penalized the manager for how much a team's performance level exceeded or undershot expectations based on the talent of the roster. Klopp and Guardiola topped the list -- with a significant gap between themselves and the next tier of coaches.

Given the 114 guilty charges against Manchester City under Guardiola, though, I think we have to go with Klopp. While Guardiola's influence on how the sport is played is undeniable, we now have to look on his Man City tenure skeptically. We know how much they outperformed what we were told they spent, but it would be foolish to blindly accept those numbers and attribute the gap purely to the Guardiola effect.

With Klopp, though, we know that he turned two clubs that were not even the richest clubs in their own leagues into two of the best teams in the world. And we know that he maintained those levels -- at both clubs -- for many seasons in a row. On top of that, both Borussia Dortmund and now Liverpool seem to have gotten worse after he left each job.

The job of the manager, simply, is to make his team better than the talent his club can afford to acquire and then to keep that improvement going even as the roster turns over. At the highest level of the sport, Klopp was better at that than any of his peers.

Could the best manager in the world save Manchester United?

What, then, might've happened if Manchester United somehow managed to hire Jurgen Klopp back in 2013 instead of David Moyes?

There are, of course, all kinds of ripple effects we could tease out -- what it would've done to German soccer, where Liverpool would've ended up, how Mohamed Salah's career would've played out, and on and on.

But I just want to focus on what it would've meant for Manchester United. We know that Liverpool benefitted from hiring Jurgen Klopp. But we also know that Jurgen Klopp benefitted from working for a club that did things like convincing him to sign Mohamed Salah instead of Julian Brandt.

Liverpool's cutting-edge front office didn't turn the club into the best team in the world, and neither did Klopp. No, it was the combo of the two that did it.

We could say similarly about Borussia Dortmund. At the time, Dortmund were one of the leaders in both youth development and identifying young stars. This meant that Klopp got the ideal kinds of talent, energetic youngsters to play his high-pressing style: Robert Lewandowski, Mats Hummels, Marco Reus, and Ilkay Gündogan -- just to name a few.

What we know about Manchester United, broadly, is that the club is an abject disaster. In terms of doing things that increase their chances of winning games, they are pretty much as bad as it gets. Since 2013, United have finished at or higher in the table than their relative Premier League revenue ranking once -- and that was last season.

While we could employ some magical thinking and convince ourselves that the only problem here is that the club can't hire the right coach, that's obviously not true. If it were, it would mean that the club that keeps firing its coaches just so happens to be doing all of the other things right.

No, the failure to find a successful long-term coach is a symptom of all of the other issues that plague the club. They've so badly underperformed their resources for over a decade; we can confidently say there is something deeply wrong with the way Manchester United tries to build its soccer teams.

So, if Klopp were the Man United coach, he wouldn't have fixed all of those problems. No, he would've had to work within that dysfunctional environment. He would've, in other words, ended up with Brandt instead of Salah -- many times over.

But let's sketch out the absolute best-case scenario for this hypothetical. Let's say that United have continued to hire "relegation-quality" managers. And let's say that Klopp's value is equivalent not just to the best player on a title team but to a true, once-in-a-generation superstar.

Neither of those things is true -- United aren't constantly hiring genuinely bad coaches, and Klopp himself would tell you that he's not worth the same as Lionel Messi -- but stretching the effect out to the extreme helps make the point.

Plus, by applying a Messi-like effect every year, we're canceling out some of the other problems with this exercise: not addressing the Manchester City situation, not subtracting points from other teams, not accounting for the increased spending power from an increased performance level, and so on.

If Klopp could've added 10 points to every Manchester United season, here's how things would've changed:

On average, United would've ended up with 76 points per season instead of 66, and their average finishing position would've been 3.8 instead of 5.3.

So, of course: things would be better if Manchester United had employed the best manager of the modern era for the last decade-plus. In this scenario, they would've finished in the top four 10 times, rather than six. Perhaps there would've been a deep Champions League run at a club that reached three finals in four seasons from 2008 to 2011 and hasn't been beyond the quarterfinals since.

But even if we granted Manchester United 13 straight seasons of consistent, transformative, incomparable, once-in-a-generation managerial performance, the team would still find itself right where it sits today: with no Premier League titles since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club.

stories.headline: Pedro Martinez appeals for MLB resolution, reflects on effects of 1994 strike
stories.summary: Pedro Martinez appealed to both MLB players and owners to find a solution to their CBA talks, saying "get something done and don't lock out baseball for the fans."
stories.body:
Hall of Fame pitcher Pedro Martinez spoke out about the looming lockout hanging over Major League Baseball, saying a resolution must be found to protect the sport and fans.

"I feel for the fans, and I know when it's good, and it's good, baseball is good right now," Martinez said Saturday, according to the Boston Herald. "So stop the crap around and get something done and don't lock out baseball for the fans."

In Boston for the Pedro Martinez Foundation's 10th annual gala, Martinez said that "honestly speaking, I'm pissed" as he appealed to both players and owners to find a solution.

"Please, for the fans, both sides, figure it out, a good way to get it done, and do not lock out baseball," Martinez said.

The current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1. MLB owners are trying to put a salary cap in place. Their latest offer, made Tuesday, would delay the implementation of the cap until 2028.

The players' union has remained steadfast against any talks of a salary cap during negotiations.

Martinez was hurt in multiple ways by a previous baseball stoppage early in his career. At the time of the 1994 strike, he was in his first season with the Montreal Expos, who had the best record in the majors at 74-40 and dreams of a World Series title when play was stopped. The cancellation of the rest of the 1994 season also kept Martinez a day away from arbitration eligibility.

"I hope the commissioner can see me and hear and the players' association hears what I have to say. I might be insignificant, but I lived it before. I experienced that before," Martinez said. "... I was one of the most punished players at that moment because I had talent, and I needed to wait until arbitration to make my money. So I hope they don't mess it up and they don't mistreat the fans."

"Back then, there was a need for other things to change, and they changed for the better. This time, there's no excuse," Martinez added in comparing the 1994 strike to today. "On both sides, not the PA, not the owners, not baseball. The fans do not deserve to be mistreated."

Martinez was a three-time Cy Young Award winner and eight-time All-Star who won the 2004 World Series with the Boston Red Sox and was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 2015.
