stories.headline: Max Verstappen's Red Bull a 'disaster to drive' despite front-row finish
stories.summary: Despite racing from 21st on the grid to second at the checkered flag, Max Verstappen said he is convinced more was possible at the São Paulo Grand Prix had his Red Bull not been "a disaster to drive."
stories.body:
Despite racing from 21st on the grid to second at the checkered flag, Max Verstappen said he is convinced more was possible at the São Paulo Grand Prix had his Red Bull not been "a disaster to drive."

The four-time champion was voted driver of the day at Interlagos after he mastered the wet conditions to overcome a grid penalty, cut through the field and finish on the podium behind race winner Lando Norris.

Verstappen made up the vast majority of his positions in the first stint of the race but reported a loss in rear grip after he switched tires at his first pit stop.

Initially it was unclear if the loss of balance was related to the changing conditions as the track dried, but after the race he was convinced the car had some sort of issue.

"My God," he said over team radio on the cooldown lap. "Doing 85% of the race with a f---ed car.

"Of course, P2 is nice but not in this way. I'm sorry, but what a disaster to drive. I've never experienced something like this in the wet or in the dry. It's really, really bad."

Verstappen started from 21st on the grid after Red Bull elected to replace his power unit ahead of qualifying, incurring a 30-place grid penalty.

Speaking in the postrace news conference, the Dutch driver said the early part of the race had been good fun, but lamented the loss in performance after his pit stop.

"When you start that far back, you need to try and, of course, to get by the guys ahead of you as quickly as you can," Verstappen said. "I do think that first stint went really, really well. We got very quickly back into the top 10.

"I think the pace wasn't bad, but as soon as I switched to the slicks, I had some extreme amount of oversteer in the car, in the high-speed corners, which made it super difficult to drive. We need to understand if something broke on the car, if there was some kind of error, loss or whatever, because this was not normal.

"I sit here, of course, very happy with second, but at the same time, I knew or I know there was more in it if the car would have been in good shape. Unfortunately, that was not the case. I actually did most of the race with a car that was not in good shape. To sit here being second, of course, is fantastic."

- Lando Norris holds off Max Verstappen to win São Paulo Grand Prix

- Mercedes completes the double with constructors' title at São Paulo Grand Prix

- Lando Norris praises McLaren for win, celebrates mastering São Paulo conditions

It was the third year in a row that Verstappen has started toward the back of the grid due to an engine penalty.

"Maybe next year, I would love, of course, to start maybe a bit further up front instead of starting from the back or the pit lane," he said. "We'll find out next year. But it's been good. In the wet, it probably also gives you a few more opportunities to get by cars, and you can do some different lines and more opportunities.

"That definitely helped me today, but we also have to understand why or what went wrong with the car as soon as we went to the slick tires. Because even when I saw back to the inter tires, at the end, the car was night and day different to my first stint, which shows that there is something wrong."

stories.headline: Premier League VAR review: Should Man United's equalizing goal have been allowed?
stories.summary: VAR often causes controversy, but how are decisions made? Our resident ref, Andy Davies, explains all.
stories.body:
The video assistant referee causes controversy every week, whether it be the Premier League, Champions League or FA Cup, but how are those decisions made and are they correct?

For the 2026-27 season, we are taking a look at the major incidents to explain the process in terms of both VAR protocol and the laws of the game. The most surprising, controversial and complicated decisions will be examined all season long right here.

Photo credit: USA Sports, NBC

Andy Davies (@andydaviesref) is a former Select Group referee, with over 12 seasons on the elite list, working across the Premier League and Championship. With extensive experience at the elite level, he has operated within the VAR space in the Premier League and offers a unique insight into the processes, rationale and protocols that are delivered on a matchday.

Did Lammens interfere with Suzuki?
Manchester United 4-4 Aston Villa (Nov. 8)
Referee: Chris Kavanagh

VAR: Craig Pawson

Time: 96 minutes

Incident: Possible foul in Manchester United's equalizing goal.

What happened: Bruno Fernandes swung in a last-chance corner kick as Man United threw every player they had on the pitch, including keeper Senne Lammens, into the penalty area.

Patrick Dorgu outjumped the Aston Villa defenders and, with keeper Zion Suzuki flapping at the ball, nodded home what seemed like a straightforward header into the net. However, Suzuki believed he was fouled by opposite number Lammens as the United No. 1 attempted to block the Villa keeper -- Lammens made contact with Suzuki while neither looking at the ball nor making any attempt to play it.

Referee Kavanagh was unmoved by the appeals, yellow-carding Suzuki for his protests and awarding the goal.

VAR decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of goal.

VAR review: VAR checked the incident and was comfortable that although Lammens clearly had intent to disturb Suzuki from having a clear path to punch the ball away by bumping into him, any contact was minimal and, more importantly, his impact on the Villa keeper was a 50-50 call. This is a ratio where VAR is not keen to get involved and will stick with the on-field decision.

Verdict: VAR were correct not to intervene in this situation as it fell short of the threshold for a clear on-field error.

Though Lammens' intention was obvious, intent is not a punishable offense, and the many replays didn't evidence enough of an impactful physical action on Suzuki that met the criteria for an intervention. However, Lammens did gamble with this play, and if referee Kavanagh had judged his action differently and awarded a late free kick to Villa, United could have few complaints.

This was a borderline call either way, and I am comfortable that the on-field decision should stick regardless of which way it fell.

Arsenal robbed of a penalty
Arsenal 1-0 Hull City (Nov. 7)
Referee: Farai Hallam

VAR: Michael Oliver

Time: 42 minutes

Incident: Penalty not awarded to Arsenal for an offside offense.

What happened: Hull's Nobel Mendy appeared to grab the shirt of Kai Havertz as the Arsenal attacker attempted to get on the end of a ball into the box.

In a confusing twist and following a VAR review, Hallam explained to the stadium that a foul action had been committed by Mendy, but Havertz was in an offside position and therefore the decision was no penalty and a restart of an indirect free kick to Hull.

VAR decision: VAR recommended an on-field review for a possible penalty to Arsenal.

VAR review: Oliver asked Hallam to review the possible penalty to Arsenal at the pitchside monitor. Once at the screen, Hallam agreed that a foul had been committed by Mendy on Havertz, however he also determined that Havertz was in an offside position when the ball was played and therefore the outcome should be a defensive free kick to Hull and not a penalty to Arsenal.

Verdict: In a complex and confusing set of circumstances, the law was incorrectly applied in this incident by Hallam. A penalty should have been the outcome, and fortunately for him and ProRef, Arsenal went on to win the game, which will dampen any fallout from the situation.

What the law says: If a player in an offside position is fouled before or without committing an offside offense, the foul is to be penalized.

I have some sympathy for Hallam, as the judgment of when a player should be judged as impacting an opponent can be open to interpretation. The positioning of Havertz and the possibility of him impacting on Mendy's next action has clearly caused a misread of the situation with the referee applying the law incorrectly.

Between the referee, Oliver and his assistant VAR, the correct outcome should have been reached, and the "live comms" will be interesting when they are released. I have been a big advocate of "live comms" being available, and this is another incident when some much-needed clarity was needed in real time, which could easily have been communicated and explained.

Liverpool denied a penalty in close game?

Liverpool vs. Arsenal

Referee: Andy Madley VAR: Stuart Attwell Time: 34 mins Incident: Possible penalty to Liverpool

What Happened: A cross into the Arsenal penalty was nearly headed toward goal by Alexander Isak, but it appeared that he was having his shirt pulled by Jurriën Timber. Referee Andy Madley was unmoved and play continued.

VAR Decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of no penalty.

VAR Review: An interesting incident for VAR to check. However, once reviewed they felt the contact fell short of a clear on-field error and cleared the decision.

Verdict / Insight: This incident will be a major talking point, and Liverpool can feel aggrieved that there was no intervention by VAR for this holding offense by Timber. In real time it looked like a foul act by Timber; however, it would have been difficult for Madley to be sure how impactful the contact was from his position at pitch level, and so a non-decision in the moment is understandable.

This season, VAR has been encouraged to set a high bar and not intervene unless an on-field decision is clearly incorrect. The man in the hub on this occasion, Stuart Attwell, clearly felt this fell short of this threshold. However, when analyzing the incident, the action by Timber was deliberate; he made no attempt to play the ball and acted with the sole motivation of impacting Isak's ability to head the ball toward goal, in which he succeeded.

When such a deliberate action has a direct impact on an opponent's ability to play the ball, this must be penalized. In my opinion, Attwell fell short of his responsibilities by not recommending an on-field review and this will go down as an error by VAR in a key Premier League match.

Did Lisandro Martinez deserve a red card?

Chelsea 2-0 Manchester United (Oct. 31)
Referee: Peter Bankes

VAR: James Bell

Time: 61 minutes

Incident: Chelsea were awarded a penalty following a VAR on-field review, and Lisandro Martínez was sent off for committing a second yellow card offense.

What happened: Man United defender Lisandro Martínez seemed to lead with his arm, contacting with the head of Chelsea's Wesley Fofana with an aerial challenge.

VAR decision: VAR recommended an on-field review for a possible penalty following the reckless challenge by Martínez on Fofana.

VAR review: With no decision on the field by referee Bankes, VAR felt uncomfortable with this challenge but could only intervene if he felt the referee had made a clear error.

Following several replays, the VAR felt that the challenge met the criteria for a clear foul and a missed incident by the referee, explaining that Martínez's act was clearly late, made no attempt to play the ball as he was facing his opponent and not the ball. And, most importantly, that the contact with his arm was a reckless action.

VAR recommended that the referee reviewed the challenge at the pitchside screen. Once at the monitor, the referee agreed with his VAR, awarded the penalty and issued a second yellow card to Martínez and sent him off.

Verdict: A correct intervention from VAR with a penalty and a second yellow card for Martínez the right outcome.

The challenge by Martínez was a poor one; by leading with his arm when making an aerial challenge and connecting with an opponent, there was always a very high chance that a yellow card would follow.

It was surprising that referee Bankes did not award the penalty in real-time, as the reckless contact by Martínez looked clear on first sight. On reflection, he'll be disappointed.

However, credit to the VAR. With the emphasis this season on minimal interventions and the pressure that surrounds their every action, it was a positive decision to recognize that this clear error needed correcting.

Why was Matheus Cunha's goal disallowed?

Time: 34 minutes

Incident: Man United's Matheus Cunha had a goal disallowed for offside.

What happened: A deep Man United corner was headed back across goal by Harry Maguire and nudged into the back of the net by Cunha. However, following a quick VAR check, Cunha was deemed to be in an offside position and the goal was disallowed.

VAR decision: A factual decision to disallow the goal for an offside offence.

VAR review: A quick check with the use of the semi-automated system (SAOT) clearly showed that Cunha's left leg was in an offside position when the ball was played by teammate Maguire.

Verdict: Not a clear or easy decision to make in real time, however the goal was correctly disallowed with the use of SAOT as Cunha's leg strayed beyond the last defender when Maguire played the ball back across the box.

No need for an on-field review by the referee in this situation, as this was a factual decision.

Why did Man United's Heaven avoid red card for two-footed tackle?

Manchester United 0-3 Bournemouth (Oct. 25)

Referee: Jarred Gillett

VAR: Paul Howard

Time: 37 minutes

Incident: Possible red card for Manchester United's Ayden Heaven

What happened: United defender Heaven flew into a challenge on Bournemouth's Evanilson. His tackle looked dangerous -- it was over the top of ball and both feet off the ground. Referee Gillett issued a yellow card to the defender, with disgruntled Bournemouth players expecting the card to be red.

VAR decision: VAR agreed with the on-field decision of a yellow card and cleared the decision as correct.

VAR review: The on-field communication from Gillett would have guided the VAR into a non-intervention as the description of the challenge was accurate to the replays reviewed.

Only a clear error or a complete misread of the challenge would have instigated an on-field review from the VAR. The referee described the challenge as reckless, showing a disregard for the safety of his opponent, and the VAR agreed with this reading of the incident and a yellow card outcome.

Verdict and insight: A correct outcome on-field and non-intervention by VAR; this challenge did not meet the threshold for a red card for a Serious Foul Play (SFP) tackle.

While an area of judgment, the tipping point between red and yellow card outcomes is normally based around level of contact on an opponent. The action by Heaven did tick some of the SFP boxes when considering a sanction, however the fact that there was no contact or any real danger to Evanilson, met a yellow criteria card.

It showed a disregard for an opponent's safety by his recklessness, but nothing more.

Should Brentford's Yarmoliuk have been sent off?
Brentford 1-2 Liverpool (Oct. 17)
Referee: John Brooks

VAR: Darren England

Time: 45 + 3 minutes

Incident: Brentford defender Yehor Yarmoliuk sent off for violent conduct.

What happened: With Liverpool setting up for a corner kick and time ticking away at the end of the first half, Brentford defender Yarmoliuk and Liverpool's Jérémy Jacquet clashed, with the Liverpool player ending up on the floor.

Following a lengthy VAR review, referee Brooks agreed with the VAR recommendation and finally sent Yarmoliuk off for committing a violent action and headbutting Jacquet.

VAR decision: VAR overturn. Red Card for violent conduct.

VAR review: England took time to recommend an on-field review, as Yarmoliuk's violent action wasn't conclusive from all replay angles. However, the penalty-area tight camera eventually gave him the clear evidence he needed to ask John Brooks to visit the pitch-side monitor and review the incident.

Verdict and insight: A correct VAR intervention in this incident, with Brentford's Yarmoliuk committing a violent action towards his opponent and the red card an expected outcome.

Like Rodrigo Bentancur's red card for Spurs in the last match round, when a player deliberately heads at an opponent and makes contact, it is very likely to end in a red card.

The four minutes it took VAR to reach the point of an on-field review is frustrating, as this should have been cleared up a lot quicker -- this will be something ProRef will need to improve moving forward.

Additionally, some discussion as to why the restart was not a penalty kick, considering it was a defender committing an offense on an attacker in the penalty area. However, the ball was not in play when the incident occurred and therefore the original corner restart was correct.

Was Gravenberch wrongly sent off in Liverpool-Man City?
Liverpool 0-3 Man City (Oct. 11)
Referee: Chris Kavanagh

VAR: Paul Howard

Time: 62 minutes

Incident: Liverpool's Ryan Gravenberch sent off for a second yellow card at a key stage in the match

What happened: Having already received a yellow card early in the match, Gravenberch fouled City's Jérémy Doku and received a second yellow card from Kavanagh.

VAR review: Newly introduced into the Premier League this season, second yellow cards can now be reviewed by VAR, but only if they are factually incorrect, and this situation does not fit this category.

Verdict and insight: Most won't like this second yellow card decision, and it will be viewed as "soft." However, Kavanagh was put into a difficult position by Gravenberch's late, clumsy challenge on Doku, which clearly denied the Man City attacker a promising attack as he had clear opportunity to attack Liverpool in a positive area of the pitch. The subsequent yellow card was not a surprise.

These situations are the worst type of situations for referees, because you really want a second-card offense to be undebatable and obvious to everyone. Technical offenses can be questioned and heavily debated, regardless of whether the referee is correct in law.

Gravenberch can feel aggrieved by his first yellow card. From the replays, it looks like the referee misjudged the contact made by the Liverpool midfielder on Elliot Anderson, and on reflection, a free kick alone would have been a better outcome. However, once a player is on a yellow card and challenges an opponent from behind, as Gravenberch did on Doku, the player is running a very high risk of receiving a second yellow if the challenge is a foul and has consequence.

Liverpool will feel hard done by, but the second yellow card was a correct call from the referee.

Should Man United have gotten a penalty at Fulham?
Fulham 1-1 Man United (Sept. 20)
Referee: Peter Bankes

VAR: Nick Hopton

Time: 86 minutes

Incident: Possible penalty to Man United for a handball

What happened: Man United's Lisandro Martínez felt he should have earned a penalty when he fired the ball at Fulham defender Calvin Bassey from close range and the ball struck Bassey's arm. The referee did not feel it was an offence and waved away the appeals for a penalty.

VAR decision: VAR agreed with the referee's interpretation of the incident, that the ball was struck at close range, defenders' arms were close to his body and within bodyline and therefore not a handball offence. VAR checked and cleared the on-filed decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: While Man United might have wanted the penalty, this was a correct on-field decision by the refereeing team and non-intervention by VAR.

This incident is a good example of how the handball law can create confusion in these types of situations. When the ball is struck at close range, the law is clear that the referee should allow play to continue if the player's hand or arm movement is the result of a natural reflex to potentially protect the player's face, and if such action does not make their body unnaturally bigger.

Additionally, if arms are within the body line and the ball would have struck the body/face this should also be taken into consideration when applying this law.

Bassey's reaction falls within this interpretation and was a good read by the on-field assistant referee, who would have led the communication in this incident.

Was Rice lucky not to be sent off at Brighton?
Brighton & Hove Albion 3-0 Arsenal (Sept. 19)
Referee: Darren England

VAR: Tim Wood

Time: 90 + 7 mins

Incident: Possible red card for Arsenal's Declan Rice

What happened: Rice picked up a late yellow card when he appeared to kick out at Brighton's Malick Yalcouyé in an off-the-ball incident.

VAR decision: The on-field decision of yellow card was checked and cleared as correct by the VAR.

In these types of situations, VAR involvement can be triggered only if they believe the on-field refereeing team missed a violent act or an act or brutality. VAR was comfortable that the action by Rice did not meet either threshold, so the check was a straightforward one.

Verdict: This frustrated act by Rice was picked up in real time by the fourth official and certainly high risk, when considering many off-the-ball, non-footballing offenses are often interpreted as a red card offense by referees and matched by the expectations of football, so Rice can consider himself fortunate. However, I am comfortable that this action in isolation was a frustrated and petulant attempt at a trip on Yalcouyé and not a violent act or act of brutality, therefore a yellow card feels like a correct and sensible outcome.

VAR would never get involved in this situation unless there was clear evidence that the on-field outcome was incorrect, so the yellow card was correctly checked and cleared. Rice is very fortunate that the original on-field interpretation of his action was only a yellow card, otherwise he would be serving a three-game ban following the international break.

Why was Phil Foden sent off in the Manchester derby?

Manchester United 0-1 Manchester City (Sept. 13)

Referee: Michael Oliver

VAR: Matt Donohue

Time: 23rd minute

Incident: Red card for Phil Foden of Manchester City

What happened: City's Foden appeared to kick out at United's Bruno Fernandes following an untidy tangle between the two players.

VAR decision: The VAR checked and confirmed the red card for violent conduct by Foden as a correct decision.

VAR review: The VAR had a straightforward check to confirm this on-field decision, as there was a clear kick out from Foden into Fernandes' body. The pictures aligned with the on-field comms from referee Michael Oliver, and this was a simple VAR process.

Verdict: Foden can have no complaints as he lost his composure in this situation.

There might be some debate around the level of contact of Foden's action. However, when you kick out in nature that Foden did in this moment, it is very likely that a red card for violent card will be the outcome, regardless of level of contact.

Referee Oliver was very quick with his decision, but his positioning was excellent, allowing him all the available information to reach his outcome. Additionally, it was a straightforward review for the VAR, and he correctly checked and cleared the decision having considered all the dynamics of the incident.

Why was Enzo Fernández not ruled offside in Man City's goal?
Manchester United 0-1 Manchester City (Sept. 13)
Time: 60th minute

Incident: City awarded controversial winning goal

What happened: Erling Haaland scored what looked like a goal that would be disallowed for offside. However, following a long VAR check, the goal was awarded and City took a significant lead.

VAR decision: The VAR overturned the on-field decision and awarded a goal, judging that Haaland was onside before he tapped into the United net.

VAR review: There were two key elements in this offside goal review. First, semi-automated technology showed that Haaland was in an onside position when the ball was crossed by his teammate. Second, the VAR had a subjective decision to make; did Man City's Enzo Fernández either play the ball or impact on Man United center back Lisandro Martínez's ability to play the ball given that Fernández was in an offside position and in front of the goal?

The VAR was comfortable that Fernández didn't meet any of the offside criteria and advised the referee that a goal should be the outcome.

Verdict: This was an incorrect decision by the VAR to award a goal to City, a controversial outcome that will create a lot of noise in the coming days.

What was correct: the factual aspect of the decision, which showed that Haaland was onside when the cross was played. Technology is now applied in these situations, and pictures clearly showed the position of the City attacker behind the leg of United's Dorgu.

However, the subjective element of this decision is where the VAR has made his error. There are two significant sections of law that the VAR did not apply in this moment, which should have resulted in a different outcome and the goal disallowed. It should be deemed an offside offense when (A) A player clearly attempts to play a ball that is close when this action impacts an opponent, or (B) A player makes an obvious action that clearly impacts the ability of an opponent to play the ball.

In this situation, Man United's Martinez was clearly impacted by the position and action of Fernández. Martinez's ability to defend the ball was certainly affected by Fernández, and this should have been recognized within the VAR review.

The process in this situation should have been an on-field review, when the referee comes across to the screen and views the incident himself. This would have been a subjective decision and therefore only the referee can make the final decision.

Soccer doesn't like what it doesn't understand, and this was a confusing situation for everyone. The incident will be viewed as a big error and ultimately game-changing.

Should Sunderland have been given a penalty vs. Arsenal?

Sunderland 0-2 Arsenal (Sept. 12)

Referee: John Brooks

VAR: Stuart Attwell

Time: 54 min

Incident: Penalty awarded to Sunderland

What happened: With the score 0-0 early in the second half, Arsenal were left frustrated as defender Ezri Konsa was adjudged to have fouled Sunderland's Dan Ballard after a Sunderland corner, and referee John Brooks pointed to the spot.

VAR decision: VAR checked and confirmed the on-field decision of a penalty kick to Sunderland.

VAR review: Brooks' live comms described Konsa's actions on Ballard as being "all over him at the near post, facing the wrong way." Having considered the communication from the referee, VAR ruled that he was accurate in his description and his rationale for awarding a penalty kick, and confirmed the decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: With the heightened profile, focus, and referees asked to be more assertive in set-play situations such as corners, there was a high chance that a small number of penalty kicks would be awarded incorrectly, and this was an example of it playing out in real-time.

From the referee's on-field position, this incident would have looked like Konsa was clumsy with his contact on Ballard. As both players fall to the ground, referee Brooks believed that it was the Arsenal player who was pulling, deliberately facing away from the ball and committing a holding offense -- the type of foul the football world was hoping would be penalized this season.

However, from the replays, it was clear that though Arsenal's Konsa engaged with Ballard with normal contact, Ballard using his left arm to pull Konsa's shirt made the Arsenal defender spin and land on the Sunderland center back. Any punishable offense was, in fact, committed by Ballard and the restart should have been a defensive free kick.

Mikel Arteta was fuming afterwards and it's difficult to understand why VAR did not intervene in this situation given the information available to him, as it was a clear but understandable on-field error by the referee -- the referee's live description of the incident did not match the replay pictures, and this should be a red flag to the VAR.

This was a poor non-intervention by VAR, and an on-field review should have been recommended.

Why was Forest's Williams denied a winner vs. Spurs?
Nottingham Forest 0-0 Tottenham (Sep. 5)
Referee: Craig Pawson

VAR: Peter Bankes

Time: 67 min

Incident: Possible handball to Forest

What happened: Forest defender Neco Williams thought he had given his team the lead as he bundled it across the Spurs goal line. However, VAR overturned the goal for a handball offense.

VAR decision: VAR checked the referee's call of a goal for Forest and determined that Williams handled the ball immediately before scoring and recommended that the goal be disallowed.

VAR review: This was a difficult review for the VAR, which involved multiple angles and replay speeds to determine if this goal should be allowed to stand.

VAR Bankes would have been uncomfortable with the way Williams bundled the ball into the goal, as there was very high chance that it had struck his arm. However, even if the contact was accidental, the law states that any touch of the arm by the goalscorer immediately before a goal must be disallowed.

The in-goal camera provided the decisive information, as it showed the ball striking the arm of Williams as he threw himself in to try and score, creating a change in trajectory of the ball and resulting in a goal -- VAR recommended to the referee that he should disallow the goal for a handball.

Verdict and insight: Not an easy process for the VAR to review. However, once you see the decisive replays from inside Spurs' goal, it is a straightforward decision for the VAR, as the law dictates the outcome.

With so much debate surrounding the Harry Maguire "handball goal" from last week -- when the ball struck the arm of Maguire before his shot was deflected into the goal off a defender, meaning Maguire was not the actual scorer -- this scenario is far clearer and the correct outcome is reached.

How new standards cost Arsenal a clear penalty
Aston Villa 0-1 Arsenal (Aug. 31)
Referee: Jarred Gillett

VAR: James Bell

Time: 90 + 9 mins

Incident: Possible penalty to Arsenal

What happened: Arsenal's Bruno Guimarães was screaming for a penalty after he was challenged from behind by Villa's Ian Maatsen inside the box. Referee Jarred Gillett waved away the appeals.

VAR decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of no penalty.

VAR review: VAR James Bell clearly applied the new "high bar" for intervention when he cleared this decision, taking the view that the referee's on-field decision not to award a penalty to Arsenal was not a clear and obvious error. After reviewing the replays, VAR quickly checked and cleared the decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: For me, this was a clear penalty kick that should've been awarded to Arsenal. I was surprised it was not given on-field by match referee Gillett, and equally surprised the VAR did not recommend a pitch-side review.

The decision by Villa's Maatsen to challenge in the nature he did, from behind with a scissor action and no opportunity to play the ball was a poor one. By making contact only with Guimarães and none on the ball, there can be little doubt that it met the threshold for a foul -- and it took place inside the penalty box.

The surprising non-intervention by VAR is a result of the Premier League's desire this season to have less involvement and only very clear errors to be corrected, with a new "higher bar" for interventions to be applied.

It's a positive principle that should result in less time spent re-litigating decisions, yes. However, this was clearly a mistake from the on-field referee not to award a penalty and, in my opinion, this was an intervention that has been missed by the VAR team.

Arsenal winning the game will cover the narrative to some degree, however, if this was a deciding moment that cost Arsenal all three points, the profile of the incident would've been significant.

The high bar will absolutely improve the game and lower the expectations from football that VAR should get involved in everything, however it is so important that clear fouls in the penalty area, like this situation, do not get overlooked when the referee has mis-read a key moment.

Why did Maguire's obvious handball not cancel goal?
Manchester United 5-2 Ipswich Town (Aug. 30)
Referee: Craig Pawson

VAR: Jarred Gillett

Time: 56th minute

Incident: Possible handball in lead-up to Man United's second goal by Harry Maguire

What happened: The ball was cleared out of Ipswich's box toward Maguire, and the ball appeared to strike the arm of Maguire. He brought the ball to his feet and struck the ball toward goal, where it then took a grave deflection from Ipswich defender Jacob Greaves before going into the goal. Following a VAR review, the goal was allowed to stand.

VAR decision and communications: The referee's call of goal for Manchester United was checked and confirmed by VAR, who deemed that Maguire was not the immediate goalscorer after an accidental handball.

VAR: "It's an own goal and the accidental handball is not punishable, so we recommend you award the goal."

VAR review: With the knowledge that the ball had clearly struck the arm of Maguire, the VAR had two key elements to consider:

(1) Was Maguire's shot on target before it struck Greaves and entered the goal? In other words: was Maguire the goalscorer?

(2) Was the handball by Maguire accidental or a punishable as an intentional handball offence?

The answers to both questions could have resulted in a different outcome, but the VAR determined that it was clearly an own goal by Greaves, meaning Maguire was not the scorer, and that the handball incident was accidental. Both details meant the ball striking the arm of Maguire was negated in law, and the VAR recommended to the referee that the goal should be awarded.

Verdict and insight: It's understandable that Ipswich Town will feel hard-done by the decision.

If Maguire had scored the goal, then his handling of the ball in the lead-up would've canceled out the goal. It's only because it took the massive deflection that changed the trajectory of the ball that Maguire's incidental handball did not result in the goal being overturned.

In truth, it was a 50/50 decision that could have fallen the other way if the judgement of VAR was a different one. But the law doesn't allow a goal to be disallowed in this situation if the handball by Maguire was judged as accidental.

The subjective nature of handball in general is a confusing element of the game, and if VAR had judged this as a punishable handball and disallowed the goal, it would certainly have been a credible outcome given the context of the situation in my opinion -- and a more comfortable outcome for football.

However, the judgement by VAR Jared Gillett was not an incorrect one, with Maguire challenging for a bouncing ball and his arms in front of his body, the ball striking his left arm can certainly be deemed as accidental. It was on this occasion, with Man United the benefactor of it in this situation, and Ipswich rightfully feeling hard done by.

Should Liverpool have been bailed out by penalty?
Newcastle United 2-2 Liverpool (Aug. 23)
Referee: Stuart Attwell

VAR: James Bell

Time: 90 + 6 mins

Incident: Penalty awarded to Liverpool for a challenge by Lewis Hall on Victor Muñoz

What happened: Liverpool's Muñoz charged into the Newcastle penalty area late into the game, and Hall made a clumsy challenge bringing the Liverpool player to the ground. Referee Stuart Attwell pointed to the spot for a late penalty for the Reds.

VAR decision and communications: The referee's call of penalty for the challenge by Hall on Muñoz was checked and confirmed by VAR.

The referee: "He doesn't play the ball. He makes clear contact."

VAR: "It's knee into thigh contact. Confirming the on-field decision of penalty."

Verdict: This was a correct decision made by referee Atwell and his assistant, and a decision I felt was clear in real-time.

In this type of situation, with an attacker moving into the penalty area at speed with the ball under control, any challenge by a defender must successfully play the ball or they run a very high risk of committing a foul.

Hall was naïve to make his clumsy challenge in the manner he did, and Muñoz was too clever for the Newcastle defender. This was a clear foul by Hall, and a penalty kick a correct outcome.

While it may feel to Newcastle fans that Liverpool were bailed out and gifted a draw after middling performance, Hall's foul was needless and to blame for Liverpool equalizing.

stories.headline: Bayern Munich's Manuel Neuer set for spell on sidelines with foot injury
stories.summary: Bayern Munich goalkeeper Manuel Neuer sustained a partial ligament tear in his right foot and will be out of action for "the time being," the club said in a statement on Sunday.
stories.body:
Bayern Munich goalkeeper Manuel Neuer sustained a partial ligament tear in his right foot and will be out of action for "the time being," the club said in a statement on Sunday.

Neuer had to go off with the injury shortly before halftime in Bayern's 2-1 Bundesliga win at Mainz on Saturday.

Bayern's statement did not give a specific length of layoff for the German goalkeeper, only stating it would be 'for the time being'.

"Manuel Neuer will be out of action for FC Bayern for the time being," the club said.

"The captain sustained a partial tendor tear in his right foot during the German record champions' 2-1 win against 1.FSV Mainz 05 on Saturday, as confirmed by an examination by the FC Bayern medical unit.

"Neuer was substitued shortly before half-time at Mainz."

Replacement goalkeeper Jonas Urbig filled in, as he has often done for the veteran Neuer this season. Urbig is viewed as Neuer's long-term successor at the club and the injury presents a chance to demonstrate he can eventually take the role.

The injury is another blow to Bayern's season following Vincent Kompany's battles with issues that saw him collapse at training. He was hospitalised and treated for meningeal irritation, which is an inflammation of the tissue around the brain or spinal cord.

Neuer has only made five league appearances this season, while the 23-year-old Urbig has also made five, including his substitute appearance Saturday.

It was a bittersweet moment for Neuer as he also became Bayern's oldest Bundesliga player at 40 years and 225 days old in the game.

stories.headline: Witness: Clase 'inside' pitch info dried up amid Mizuhara case fallout
stories.summary: A witness said that the inside info he used to bet on Clase pitches dried up due to increased scrutiny from the scandal involving Shohei Ohtani's interpreter.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- A government witness testified Friday in the federal trial of Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz that the inside information he used to bet regularly on Clase pitches in 2023 dried up the next season due to increased scrutiny from the gambling scandal involving Shohei Ohtani's interpreter at the time.

Luis de Aza Baez said he placed dozens of bets and won thousands of dollars by wagering on the velocity of select Clase pitches during the 2023 season, "because I had inside information." Clase is accused of conspiring with bettors to rig 18 pitches over three seasons.

De Aza Baez said that when he asked for more information on Clase pitches in 2024, he was told that because of "what was going on with Ohtani, there was no more information like that."

Ohtani, the Los Angeles Dodgers' superstar, came under scrutiny in March 2024 after ESPN reported that millions of dollars had been sent from his bank account to an illegal bookmaking operation. His longtime interpreter, Ippei Mizuhara, later pleaded guilty to stealing nearly $17 million from Ohtani to pay off gambling debts and is currently in prison. Ohtani was cleared of any wrongdoing.

De Aza Baez, who worked as an Uber driver, told prosecutors that he began receiving information about the pitches from Enoc Pena, an associate of Clase's, in 2023. De Aza Baez said the tips often came through a group chat titled "Uber Inc." that Pena started and included other men who have been referenced in the case and also worked for the ride-share company in Massachusetts at the time.

Prosecutors showed a screenshot of a text message Clase allegedly sent to Pena on Sept. 30, 2023, when the Guardians were scheduled to play the Detroit Tigers, that talked about "killing the first two chickens." De Aza Baez said the message was instructions to bet on a Clase pitch to the third batter of an inning, but only if Clase had retired the first two batters. Clase did not appear in the game.

Clase's defense has argued that mentions of roosters and chickens in such communications often were referencing cockfighting, a legal activity in the Dominican Republic, where Clase and others in the case are from.

De Aza Baez said he became friends with Pena as well as Robinson Vásquez Germosen and Luis Arismendy Paca Méndez, who are co-defendants in the case, while they were all living in Nantucket, Massachusetts. Paca Méndez, who has pleaded not guilty, is not participating in the trial after being extradited from the Dominican Republic to the U.S. on Oct. 19.

De Aza Baez said he met Clase when Vásquez and Pena brought the pitcher to his house for a birthday party on April 28, 2023, in Winthrop, Massachusetts, where De Aza Baez had moved. He met Clase again a few days later at a relative's house. Prosecutors showed a video of the gathering, with Clase playing dominoes on a table featuring a Boston Red Sox logo. The Guardians were in town for a series against the Red Sox.

De Aza Baez said he never received any information directly from Clase, only from Pena. De Aza Baez said he did not have an agreement with Pena but gave him money because he "almost always" won using the information to bet on Clase's pitches. De Aza Baez acknowledged opening a DraftKings betting account under his wife's name to increase the amount he could wager and win on his Clase bets. De Aza Baez also said he included the Clase pitch bets in parlays to maximize payouts.

De Aza Baez acknowledged that he had agreed with the government to forfeit $69,000 from his winning bets on Clase and would "tell the truth" in exchange for prosecutors dropping a wire fraud charge related to the case.

Clase, Ortiz and Vásquez have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges of wire and honest services fraud, sports bribery and money laundering.

"Our defense is the same today as it was in opening: This is a case about big talk and small bets," Vásquez's attorney Todd Spodek told ESPN after Friday's hearing. "We're confident leaving that judgment to the jury."

The trial will continue next Thursday in Brooklyn.

stories.headline: Kaick, Dallas win 3-1, eliminate Rapids from playoff contention
stories.summary: - Kaick Ferreira, known simply as "Kaick", scored the go-ahead goal in the 88th and FC Dallas beat Colorado 3-1 on Saturday night to eliminati the Rapids from playoff contention.
stories.body:
FRISCO, Texas -- Kaick Ferreira, known simply as "Kaick", scored the go-ahead goal in the 88th and FC Dallas beat Colorado 3-1 on Saturday night to eliminati the Rapids from playoff contention.

Colorado (12-15-7) could have secured a spot in the MLS Cup playoffs with a win.

Dallas (16-8-10) clinched the No. 2 seed in the Western Conference and plays seventh-seeded Portland in the best-of-three first round.

Kaick cut back to evade a defender and blasted a shot from the top of the penalty box under the crossbar and inside the right post that made it 2-1.

Joaquín Valiente put away a first-touch shot, off a cross played by Kaick, that made it 1-1 in the 75th minute and Santiago Moreno capped the scoring in the second minute of stoppage time.

Morgan Whittaker scored a goal for the fourth consecutive game for the Rapids. Nico Hansen had seven saves.

Whittaker, on the counter-attack, put away a first-touch shot off a cross from Georgi Minoungou that gave Colorado a 1-0 lead in the 47th minute. Minoungou, who subbed on to begin the second half, has four assists in the past three games.

Up next Colorado: Season completes.

Dallas: Hosts Portland for Game 1.

stories.headline: How the Atlanta Dream turned their franchise around in just five years
stories.summary: Five years ago, the Dream were the second-worst team in the WNBA -- making their Finals run all the more remarkable.
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Just five years ago, the idea of the Atlanta Dream competing for the WNBA championship trophy would have seemed as unlikely as a rebound landing untouched next to Angel Reese.

So finishing within one victory of a title, as the Dream did in the WNBA Finals last week, says a lot about just how far the franchise has come since 2021. Even without the 2026 championship, what the Dream did in revitalizing their franchise is a story that shouldn't be lost in Golden State's celebration. Five years ago, the Dream were a mess. Now, they're contenders. That's something other WNBA franchises can look to.

"It's remarkable, really," Atlanta coach Karl Smesko said.

Consider how far the franchise was from this in 2021.

That was the year the Dream moved to Gateway Center Arena -- the smallest venue in the WNBA at 3,500 seats -- because too much of their longtime larger home (State Farm Arena, capacity 17,608) was vacant during games. The Dream had three different coaches that year, one resigning just before the season began to take a college job. Chennedy Carter, their lottery-pick selection from 2020, was suspended in July and never returned. They finished in second-to-last place in the WNBA at 8-24.

The team's most notable moment came not on court, but in a viral video of two Dream players throwing punches by a food truck outside an Atlanta nightclub.

Those were the low points. But behind the scenes, two big moves in 2021 helped spark a turnaround: an ownership change, led by real estate investor Larry Gottesdiener, and a new general manager, Dan Padover.

Reese was then a college sophomore with huge goals for her future. But it wasn't until this April that she knew those plans would intersect with the Dream.

"When I play with joy and I'm surrounded by people that just genuinely make me happy, I think I'm at my best," Reese said. "The organization has poured into me. To be in my third year [in the WNBA], this is obviously the best situation I've ever been in."

And even as Reese and teammates Jordin Canada and Allisha Gray sat somberly in the Dream's postgame news conference after Game 7, the joyful sounds of Ballhalla's celebration audible, they looked dissatisfied but not devastated.

"They changed my life," Reese said of the Atlanta players and staff. "And I'm just so grateful for them."

A 2008 EXPANSION TEAM, the Dream's first title hopes were led by another Angel -- 2009 No. 1 pick Angel McCoughtry. She led the Dream to the Finals in 2010, 2011 and 2013, but they were swept each time.

The Dream then missed the playoffs six of the next nine years. They won a then-franchise record 23 games in 2018, but lost McCoughtry to a knee injury Aug. 7 and lost 3-2 in the semifinals.

Without McCoughtry in 2019, the Dream averaged just 4,270 fans for home games, necessitating the move from State Farm Arena. That relocation was delayed a year because of the COVID-19 pandemic, when the 2020 season was in a "bubble" in Bradenton, Florida. By then, McCoughtry had left in free agency for Las Vegas.

The Dream's leadership became a focus for all WNBA players in the bubble when co-owner Kelly Loeffler sent a letter to commissioner Cathy Engelbert opposing the league's decision to display "Black Lives Matter" logos on the courts in Bradenton. Loeffler wrote "we need less -- not more -- politics in sports."

Loeffler was involved in a political race at the time, seeking to hold her U.S. Senate seat. The divide mushroomed into WNBA players campaigning for her opponent, Raphael Warnock.

"Being on the outside of the Dream looking in then, during that time everybody was rallying around them," said guard Jordin Canada, then with the Seattle Storm, of the bubble activism against Loeffler's continued ownership. "We wanted what was best for them and the W as a whole, and to see that transition into a more positive direction."

The situation was untenable, and the franchise was sold in February 2021 to Gottesdiener's group, which included former WNBA player Renee Montgomery.

"I believed the WNBA was an extraordinary opportunity, not just to grow the game of basketball," Gottesdiener said, "but to demonstrate what's possible when you invest in women."

Padover, who joined the Dream in October 2021, had worked for the Las Vegas Aces for three years, helping build the team that would become a three-time champion. He went from a franchise a step from the top to one with nowhere to go but up.

Padover started his WNBA career as a video coordinator with the New York Liberty in 2012, and he has credited former coach and GM Bill Laimbeer for helping him develop into a team executive. He cites this key from Laimbeer.

"If you can get your organization organized and you can take care of the players, you can start to establish yourself as a place that is respected," Padover said. "Under previous ownership, I think we were disorganized, and we didn't really have an identity.

"When I got here the goal was, 'Let's turn Atlanta back into a franchise that's respected throughout the WNBA community, one piece at a time, and that will allow us to be able to build something.' We started with things like player housing, staffing, and medical and player development."

THE OTHER PIECE was putting the right players and coaches in the building. Padover, who has been named the league's executive of the year three times, put his trade wizardry to use. He dealt the Nos. 3 and 14 picks in the 2022 draft and a 2023 pick swap to Washington for the No. 1 pick in 2022 to select Rhyne Howard.

"It was a huge boost of confidence," Howard said. "Obviously, when you get drafted, that means the team wants you. But to do it in the way that they did -- trading up to get me like that -- put no doubt in my mind that I was a piece that they were looking for to start this new journey, to start this new outcome that we're having."

The 6-foot-2 guard was Rookie of the Year and has since been a four-time All-Star. She averaged 17.7 points in the regular season this year and 16.3 in the playoffs. Howard won't recall Game 7 fondly -- she was limited to six points on 3-of-14 shooting -- but she took noticeable steps forward as a player in 2026, especially on defense.

Padover also got the steal of the second round in 2022 with forward Naz Hillmon, who became a full-time starter this season and has played more WNBA games than anyone from that draft class.

Subsequent huge deals came for guards Gray (2023) and Canada (2024).

"One of the things that I definitely took from Bill was not to be skittish to give up things in trades," Padover said. "If you're doing it to get a great player, it's always worth it, and don't be afraid to do that."

One of Padover's biggest moves in 2025 was bringing in Smesko, who had spent most of his career as a college coach, including 17 years at Florida Gulf Coast.

"Obviously, there was a changing landscape in college basketball, and I was at the point where a new challenge was needed," Smesko said of his decision to move to the WNBA. "It was Atlanta, and I love the city. And I thought there was the makings of a core that could compete for a championship."

Atlanta went 30-14 last season but lost in the first round of the playoffs. Padover used a trade to acquire the last key component. On April 6, the Dream obtained Reese from the Chicago Sky for future draft picks. Reese had become disillusioned with the Sky's direction and voiced her concerns near the end of the 2025 season. She believed in the Dream's vision, just as the players obtained before her did.

"I feel like the organization has gotten to a point where players want to come play for Atlanta," Gray said. "To be able to get Angel just speaks volumes of how the organization is run and how it really cares for players. The city of Atlanta is great. Great culture. The games just feel like one big family cookout, and everybody's welcome."

Reese proved to be the final and most essential ingredient. Other than a five-game skid June 24-July 4, the Dream -- who also added veteran DeWanna Bonner late in the season -- stayed consistent, finishing 30-14 again. Reese had the best offensive year of her career, averaging 16.4 points, plus 12.1 rebounds.

"She's made me look good all season long," Howard said. "And I'm sure she's going to continue to do that for the rest of her time here. Shoutout to her for coming in and being bought in. She's handled every challenge that we've thrown at her with grace."

This year's Finals games in Atlanta didn't come without hurdles -- facility conflicts with State Farm Arena meant one Finals game had to be moved up a day and another had to be played at 12:30 p.m. ET on a Thursday. But even that early game was joyful and loud, a full house of fans skipping work and school to cheer on the Dream in a must-win Game 6.

Next year, the Dream moves back to State Farm Arena full time, playing all 25 regular-season home games there.

And as disappointed as the Dream were after losing Game 7, they also immediately expressed excitement about the 2027 season.

"Just because we didn't win today doesn't mean that we won't be champions in the future," Reese said.

Those words weren't just platitudes after a disappointing ending. Next year, with every starter already signed to return, the Dream could at last win that elusive title.

"I like our chemistry and just the sisterhood that we have as a team," said Gray, who played every Finals game despite sustaining an injury on her shooting hand in the semifinals. "We actually love each other and enjoy being around each other."

stories.headline: Kangaroos into World Cup final after thrashing Samoa
stories.summary: Australia have thrashed Samoa by 32 points to book a Rugby League World Cup final clash with New Zealand.
stories.body:
A backflipping Reece Walsh has helped put Australia within touching distance of their fourth-straight World Cup crown as the Kangaroos dismantled Samoa 44-12 in their semi-final.

In their most complete performance of the tournament to date, Kevin Walters' outfit put an ill-disciplined Samoan side to the sword, running in eight tries at Sydney's Allianz Stadium on Sunday night.

Led by fullback Walsh, who scored a hat-trick, the Kangaroos rarely looked troubled.

Australia will face New Zealand at Suncorp Stadium in Brisbane in next Sunday's final as they look to extend their stranglehold on the World Cup that stretches back to 2013.

"That's just Reece, he's always brings up something that you don't expect and the backflip was no different," said Walters.

"Tonight was a really good performance. I still think there's a bit more in us too, so that's exciting.

"Our middle forwards, I thought they stood up really well, they've been questioned and criticised by some people but not within our group."

As fluent as Australia were, Samoa were all at sea in one of their most underwhelming showings since their surprise run to the 2022 final.

With a side stacked with NRL talent and a groundswell of support from their diaspora community, Samoa have a realistic hope of breaking international rugby league's glass ceiling in the years to come.

But on Sunday they made nine errors and gave up 12 set restarts or penalties, while prop Spencer Leniu was sin-binned for dissent late in a disastrous first half.

Samoan coach Ben Gardiner claimed Australia benefited from "homeground calls".

"On the back of some of the penalties that were given, we just didn't react very well on the back of it," said Gardiner.

"Then it was one thing into another and then a try, so it made it really difficult to be able to fight back from that."

After a lively pre-game siva tau where they came face to face with the Kangaroos, Samoa were first on the board when Stephen Crichton kicked a fourth minute penalty.

But it was all one-way traffic from then on as Australia asserted their dominance, starting when Tom Dearden scythed through some feeble defence off a scrum play to put the home side on the board.

Jacob Preston pinballed his way over from close range before Tom Trbojevic, Walsh and Bradman Best all crossed to push the Kangaroos out to a 26-2 halftime lead.

Walsh - chosen ahead of James Tedesco for the starting No. 1 spot - celebrated his try with a backflip.

"He probably didn't need to do that but he did it for some sick kids," Walters explained.

But he was left red-faced soon after halftime when he leapt to claim a Samoa bomb, which Crichton scooped up to score.

The Brisbane fullback soon made amends by slaloming his way through the Samoan defence and palming off Brian To'o to add his second.

Izack Tago barged his way over as Samoa showed something of a fightback.

But again, Walsh was the man in the right place at the right time.

The fullback backed up a Cameron Munster break to add his third before having a hand in Australia's final try to winger Jack Bostock.
